claims.statement: There is a rich ecosystem of economists embracing the “messy life” approach, though they are often marginalized by mainstream departments.
These economists understand network effects: how technologies spread through social connections rather than economic incentives alone.
These economists study cultural adaptation: how societies reshape technologies rather than just being passively affected by them.
These economists recognize emergent phenomena: how new forms of organization emerge from complex social interactions.
These economists value ethnographic insight: they spend time observing how systems actually work rather than just modeling them.
These economists embrace methodological pluralism: they use whatever methods work rather than being constrained by mathematical formalism.
These economists face difficulty publishing in top economics journals.
These economists are often relegated to policy schools, business schools, or other departments.
These economists have less influence on mainstream economic thinking.
These economists are often better at predicting real-world outcomes.
These economists would likely recognize that AI + RAG + agentic behavior + cultural adaptation leads to much more transformation than Acemoglu’s 5% prediction.
Ha‑Joon Chang challenges free‑market orthodoxy with cultural and historical analysis.
Ha‑Joon Chang shows how informal institutions shape economic development.
Dani Rodrik’s “Economics Rules” advocates for methodological pluralism.
Dani Rodrik emphasizes context‑dependency and local institutional knowledge.
Dani Rodrik argues against one‑size‑fits‑all economic models.
Matthew Jackson is a pioneer in social network economics.
Matthew Jackson’s “The Human Network” shows how informal connections drive economic outcomes.
Brian Arthur is the founder of complexity economics.
Brian Arthur shows how technologies evolve through cultural and network processes.
César Hidalgo studies how knowledge flows through social networks.
César Hidalgo’s work is data‑driven but socially informed.
Sendhil Mullainathan studies how cultural context shapes economic behavior.
Sendhil Mullainathan’s “Scarcity” shows how social conditions affect cognitive capacity.
Raghuram Rajan’s “The Third Pillar” emphasizes community and social institutions.
James Robinson (University of Chicago) is Acemoglu's frequent co-author but more open to informal institutions.
James Robinson's "The Narrow Corridor" explores how societies balance state and social power.
James Robinson is more ethnographically informed than Acemoglu.
Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo (MIT) are development economists who spend time on the ground.
Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo's "Good Economics for Hard Times" incorporates cultural and social factors.
Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo are Nobel winners who actually listen to people they study.
Steve Keen (Kingston University) incorporates network effects and cultural dynamics in Post-Keynesian economics.
Steve Keen's "Debunking Economics" critiques mathematical formalism.
Stephanie Kelton (Stony Brook) is a Modern Monetary Theory advocate emphasizing how political and social factors shape economic policy.
Herman Daly (University of Maryland) studies the economy as embedded in social and ecological systems in Ecological Economics.
Herman Daly emphasizes cultural values and social cooperation.
Herman Daly's "Beyond Growth" integrates social and environmental factors.
Mark Granovetter (Stanford Sociology) pioneered "embeddedness" theory showing how informal networks drive economic outcomes.
Viviana Zelizer (Princeton Sociology) studies how cultural meanings shape economic behavior.
Viviana Zelizer's "Purchase of Intimacy" shows how social relationships and economics intertwine.
Richard Swedberg (Cornell Sociology) is an economic sociology pioneer who studies how entrepreneurship emerges from social networks.
Fernando Fajnzylber (ECLAC tradition) emphasizes how cultural and institutional factors shape development in Latin American Structuralism.
Fernando Fajnzylber uses a network-based approach to industrial development.
Justin Yifu Lin (Peking University) studies how informal institutions guide China's development in Chinese Institutional Economics.
Justin Yifu Lin's "Demystifying the Chinese Economy" shows cultural adaptation of markets.
Benno Ndulu (University of Cape Town) studies how traditional institutions interact with modern markets in African Development Economics.
Benno Ndulu emphasizes social networks and cultural practices.
Shoshana Zuboff (Harvard Business School emeritus) studies how technology shapes social behavior in "The Age of Surveillance Capitalism" in Digital Economics.
Nick Srnicek (King's College London) studies how digital networks reshape economics in "Platform Capitalism" in Platform Economics.
Raj Chetty (Harvard) uses big data to study how social networks affect economic mobility in Inequality & Social Dynamics.
